title: Sullivan v. O’Connor
summary: An unsuccessful promised nose improvement supported damages for expenses, worsening, and the additional operation; the preserved issues did not require a single exclusive choice between reliance and expectation.
notes:
Court: Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts (1973).

The following problems vary operative pain, improvement, deterioration, expenses, and opportunities forgone. Keep an item’s place in a damages calculation separate from the legal basis for enforcing the promise.

sections.Parties: Sullivan, a professional entertainer, sued O’Connor, the surgeon who undertook to improve the appearance of her nose.
sections.Material Facts: The alleged agreement contemplated two operations and an improved appearance. Three operations left Sullivan worse off. Her out-of-pocket expenses were $622.65. The jury awarded $13,500 on the contract count and found for the surgeon on negligence.
sections.Procedural History: The surgeon challenged the inclusion of damages beyond expenses. Sullivan waived claims for the promised improvement and the pain of the first two operations. The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts upheld the award on the issues preserved for review.
sections.Issue: Can the patient recover for deterioration and additional pain following breach of a promised surgical result, even though the surgeon was not negligent? What interests do those damages protect?
sections.Holding: The challenged recovery was permissible. Expenses, worsening of the patient’s condition, associated distress, and the pain of the third operation could be recovered in this setting. The court did not require Sullivan to receive only a refund.
sections.Reasoning: Negligence and breach of a contractual undertaking differ. The opinion discusses the possible harshness of full expectation awards in medical cases and the availability of reliance relief. On the posture presented, deterioration and the third operation’s pain are compatible with either approach. The original operative pain might figure in reliance but was waived; the value of the promised improvement would be an expectation component but was also waived. Reading the decision as selecting reliance for every medical-promise case would exceed what these preserved issues establish.
